WHAT THE DATA SAYS

Preparing the analysis…

TRANSPARENT BY DESIGN

Every result has a method.

Built for students, educators, and environmental data explorers. This is a reproducible investigation tool, with assumptions visible alongside the result.

  1. 01

    Start with real data

    Four downloaded NASA POWER snapshots contain monthly meteorological values from 1981–2025. MERRA-2 is reanalysis: observations combined with a model, on an approximately 0.5° × 0.625° grid.

  2. 02

    Use complete years

    Only years with all 12 valid months enter NASA analyses. Temperature and humidity use day-weighted annual means. Precipitation sums monthly rates × days to obtain annual millimetres.

  3. 03

    Measure the trend

    Ordinary least squares estimates the change per decade. A two-sided Student t test and 95% slope interval describe evidence for a non-zero linear trend. R² reports fit, not causality.

  4. 04

    Read the limits

    The test assumes independent residuals, constant variance, and an approximately linear relationship; small-sample inference assumes normal residuals. Serial correlation, many tests, short windows, and changing datasets can affect conclusions.

Method adapted from the regional time-series and least-squares analysis in Acker et al. (2009), a NASA resource listed for this challenge. A single-predictor ANOVA F test is equivalent to the slope t test (F = t²). The NASA POWER data here are separate from that paper’s SeaWiFS measurements. Annual aggregation here uses physical day weights, rather than the paper’s monthly-anomaly method. The shaded chart interval is for the fitted mean, and excludes measurement and model uncertainty.
